config.title: Build typed micro frontend contract

intro.title: Build typed micro frontend contract
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed contract for a micro frontend, which defines the structure and rules for how different parts of a web application communicate. You will learn to use TypeScript interfaces to create a clear, type-safe agreement between components, ensuring data is passed correctly. The main technologies involved are TypeScript's type system and interface constructs. By the end, you'll have a reusable contract that prevents errors and improves collaboration in a micro frontend architecture.
intro.usecase: Typed micro frontend contracts are essential in large-scale applications like e-commerce platforms, where multiple teams independently build components like product listings, shopping carts, and checkout flows. These contracts ensure that components like dashboard widgets, data filters, or modal dialogs communicate reliably across different frameworks. For example, a typed contract guarantees that a search filter component passes correctly formatted data to a results panel, preventing runtime errors. This pattern is crucial in enterprise applications where modularity and type safety reduce integration bugs and streamline team collaboration.

objectives: Construct a TypeScript interface to define the structure of a micro frontend contract
Implement a concrete class that fulfills the contract interface with typed properties and methods
Apply type annotations to enforce data consistency between micro frontend components
Configure a module export to expose the typed contract for external consumption
Initialize a contract instance with specific data that adheres to the defined interface
Manipulate the contract by adding validation logic to its methods
Integrate the typed contract into a mock host application to verify interoperability

steps.title: Import TypeScript and create a types file
steps.instruction: Create a new TypeScript file named 'contract-types.ts' to hold all type definitions for the micro frontend contract.
steps.hint: In your project, create a new file with the .ts extension and name it 'contract-types.ts'. This file will be dedicated to TypeScript type definitions.
steps.seedCode: // Create a new TypeScript file named 'contract-types.ts'
steps.expectedOutcome: A new TypeScript file named 'contract-types.ts' is created in your project directory.
successCriteria: The file 'contract-types.ts' exists and is ready to contain type definitions for the micro frontend contract.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a file, but make sure it's named exactly 'contract-types.ts' with the .ts extension for TypeScript.
steps.feedbackWrong: The file wasn't created correctly. Please create a new TypeScript file named 'contract-types.ts' in your project.

steps.title: Define the MicroFrontendProps interface
steps.instruction: In the 'contract-types.ts' file, define an interface named 'MicroFrontendProps' to establish the typed contract between the host and micro frontend.
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and curly braces to define properties.
steps.seedCode:
// Create a new TypeScript file named 'contract-types.ts'

// Define the MicroFrontendProps interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: The MicroFrontendProps interface is defined with the correct name, ready to have properties added in the next step.
successCriteria: The interface named 'MicroFrontendProps' is properly defined in the TypeScript file.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're using the exact interface name 'MicroFrontendProps' and the proper TypeScript syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Remember to use the 'interface' keyword followed by 'MicroFrontendProps' and curly braces.

steps.title: Add required props to the interface
steps.instruction: Add two required properties to the MicroFrontendProps interface: 'id' of type string and 'initialData' of type any.
steps.hint: Add the properties inside the interface body, separated by a semicolon or newline.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MicroFrontendProps interface now includes 'id' and 'initialData' as required properties.
successCriteria: The MicroFrontendProps interface has both 'id: string' and 'initialData: any' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some properties, but make sure both 'id' (string) and 'initialData' (any) are present.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface is missing one or both required properties. Check the instruction again.

steps.title: Add optional props with default values
steps.instruction: Add two optional properties to the MicroFrontendProps interface: 'theme' (string) and 'debugMode' (boolean). Use the TypeScript optional property syntax with a question mark.
steps.hint: Optional properties in TypeScript are defined by adding a '?' after the property name. For example: 'propertyName?: type'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MicroFrontendProps interface now includes optional 'theme' and 'debugMode' properties with proper TypeScript types.
successCriteria: The interface has 'theme?: string' and 'debugMode?: boolean' properties defined.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added some optional properties, but make sure both 'theme?: string' and 'debugMode?: boolean' are present in the interface.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface should include both optional properties: 'theme?: string' and 'debugMode?: boolean'. Check that you're using the correct TypeScript optional property syntax.

steps.title: Define event callback types
steps.instruction: Inside the MicroFrontendProps interface, add two callback function properties: 'onDataUpdate' (a function that receives data of type 'any') and 'onError' (a function that receives an Error object).
steps.hint: Remember to use proper TypeScript syntax for function types. For example: 'onDataUpdate: (data: any) => void'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MicroFrontendProps interface will include typed callback functions for handling data updates and errors.
successCriteria: The MicroFrontendProps interface contains 'onDataUpdate: (data: any) => void' and 'onError: (error: Error) => void' properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that both callback properties are correctly typed. Make sure 'onDataUpdate' accepts 'any' data and 'onError' accepts an 'Error' object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface doesn't have the required callback properties. Remember to add 'onDataUpdate' and 'onError' with proper function type annotations.

steps.title: Create the MicroFrontendComponent type
steps.instruction: Define a type alias named 'MicroFrontendComponent' that represents a React functional component accepting MicroFrontendProps.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword to create a type alias. The type should be a React component that takes MicroFrontendProps as its props.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: a type for a button component
type ButtonComponent = React.FC<ButtonProps>;
steps.expectedOutcome: A type alias 'MicroFrontendComponent' is created, typed as a React functional component that accepts MicroFrontendProps.
successCriteria: The type alias 'MicroFrontendComponent' is defined as a React functional component type with MicroFrontendProps as its props.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're creating a type alias named 'MicroFrontendComponent' that's typed as a React functional component accepting MicroFrontendProps.
steps.feedbackWrong: define a type alias named 'MicroFrontendComponent' representing a React functional component that takes MicroFrontendProps.

steps.title: Define the configuration interface
steps.instruction: Create an interface named 'MicroFrontendConfig' with three properties: 'version' (string), 'apiEndpoint' (string), and 'features' (string array).
steps.hint: Define the interface after the existing code. Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the name and property definitions.
steps.expectedOutcome: The MicroFrontendConfig interface is defined with the required typed properties.
successCriteria: The MicroFrontendConfig interface exists with 'version' (string), 'apiEndpoint' (string), and 'features' (string[]) properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the interface, but check that all three properties are included with the correct types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Ensure you create 'MicroFrontendConfig' with the three specified properties.

steps.title: Create a union type for status
steps.instruction: Define a type named 'MicroFrontendStatus' as a union of string literals: 'loading', 'ready', 'error', and 'idle'.
steps.hint: Use the 'type' keyword followed by the type name and the union operator '|' between each string literal value.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: union type for status values
type AppStatus = 'pending' | 'active' | 'inactive' | 'archived';
steps.expectedOutcome: A union type 'MicroFrontendStatus' with four possible string literal values is added to the file.
successCriteria: The 'MicroFrontendStatus' type is defined as a union of 'loading', 'ready', 'error', and 'idle'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that your union type includes all four required string literals: 'loading', 'ready', 'error', and 'idle'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The union type definition is missing or incorrect. Make sure to use the 'type' keyword and the union operator '|' between each string literal.

steps.title: Export all types from the file
steps.instruction: Add the `export` keyword before each type and interface definition to make them available for import in other files.
steps.hint: Place `export` before `interface`, `type`, or `union` to make that definition exportable.
steps.expectedOutcome: All type definitions are exported from the file.
successCriteria: The MicroFrontendProps interface, MicroFrontendComponent type, MicroFrontendConfig interface, and MicroFrontendStatus union type are exported.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've exported some types, but not all. Make sure to export each interface and type definition.
steps.feedbackWrong: No types were exported. Add the `export` keyword before each type definition.

steps.title: Create a sample implementation using the types
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named 'SampleMicroFrontend' that uses the MicroFrontendProps interface and returns a simple div with the text 'Sample Micro Frontend'.
steps.hint: Define a component that accepts props of type MicroFrontendProps and returns JSX. You can use either a function declaration or arrow function.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named 'SampleMicroFrontend' is created that uses the MicroFrontendProps interface and returns JSX.
successCriteria: The component is named 'SampleMicroFrontend', accepts props of type MicroFrontendProps, and returns a div with the text 'Sample Micro Frontend'.
